items.headline: OpenAI shows three staff the door over alleged information misuse
items.dek: Two safety researchers and a program manager dismissed, company denies retaliation for raising concerns
items.author: Carly Page
items.caption: Headline, dek and lede: "OpenAI has fired two safety researchers and a program manager for allegedly mishandling sensitive company information."
items.notes: Only outlet found describing the three as "two safety researchers and a program manager" (WSJ/AFP/Cybernews: Korbak on the safety team; Wang and Balesni on alignment). The Register does not name them. Published Fri 02 Oct 2026 13:05 UTC. Page also lists related headline "OpenAI alerts 100+ orgs that its 'misaligned models' attempted to break in - or worse".

items.headline: OpenAI statement + denial of retaliation (The Register)
items.dek: "We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," an OpenAI spokesperson said. "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work." ... At least some of the information was allegedly shared with an outside organization that evaluates AI systems. OpenAI said its investigation found other misconduct beyond that disclosure, but has not described it or identified the organization. ... The ChatGPT creator said the employees were not dismissed for raising AI safety concerns.
items.author: Carly Page
items.caption: OpenAI's stated reason (policy violation on handling sensitive info) and its denial that safety concerns were the reason.
items.notes: The "not dismissed for raising AI safety concerns" line is The Register's paraphrase of OpenAI, not a direct quote.

items.headline: OpenAI cuts ties with 3 safety researchers, WSJ reports
items.author: Aditya Mehta
items.caption: Hero + headline, byline "11:14 AM PDT - October 1, 2026".
items.notes: Written before the WSJ added names; says "The report did not name the researchers, the organization, or the information involved."

items.headline: TechCrunch: OpenAI statement, NYT context, and "unclear whether ... raised concerns through internal channels"
items.dek: "It’s unclear whether the three researchers raised concerns through internal channels before allegedly sharing information outside the organization." ... The departures come two days after The New York Times reported that OpenAI executives had brushed aside employees’ warnings about its safety practices ... An OpenAI spokesperson told the Times the company takes security concerns seriously and has internal channels for reporting safety issues, while saying it recognized "a need to move faster." ... This isn’t the first time OpenAI has dismissed researchers over alleged information sharing. In 2024, the company fired researchers Leopold Aschenbrenner and Pavel Izmailov over alleged leaks, The Information reported.
items.author: Aditya Mehta
items.caption: Body text with OpenAI statement and the 2024 precedent.
items.notes: Text is verbatim from the loaded page. The 2024-precedent sentence is below this crop (further down the article).

items.headline: OpenAI Ousts Three Safety Researchers for Allegedly Mishandling ‘Sensitive Information’

items.headline: ‘Looks Like They’re Firing Whistleblowers’: Alarm as OpenAI Reportedly Ousts Safety Experts
items.dek: “Sam Altman says we need to slow down development to ensure the safety of humanity,” one campaigner said of OpenAI’s CEO. “Yet he is allegedly firing the very people hired to keep us safe.”
items.author: Brett Wilkins
items.caption: Progressive outlet; headline quotes Rep. Greg Casar; dek quotes Shaunna Thomas of Guardrails Alliance (a super PAC).
items.notes: This is the origin of the "whistleblowers" framing: it is advocacy/critic framing ("allegedly"), not OpenAI's or WSJ's. Body: "The Journal's Maxwell Zeff - who authored the report with Keach Hagey and Berber Jin - subsequently identified the three safety team members as Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni." Casar: "Looks like they're firing whistleblowers ... What are they hiding?" "I'll be sending OpenAI a demand for transparency."

items.headline: OpenAI fires three staff for mishandling 'sensitive' info
items.dek: ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has said that it has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling "sensitive information" and violating company policies, including work that involved an external organisation that evaluates artificial intelligence models.
items.author: AFP
items.caption: "Updated / Friday, 2 Oct 2026 10:17". Caption under photo: "The San Francisco-based AI lab did not confirm the identities of the staff members".
items.notes: AFP: "at least two of the employees worked on safety and alignment, according to the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg."

items.headline: AFP: the three researchers' own public posts before the firing
items.dek: "i am at OpenAI and i think AI is >10% likely to kill all humans," Mr Balesni posted on 10 September ... "I'm quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does. I am very happy that Im allowed to say 'I'm quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does'," Mr Korbak wrote on 11 September. "It's hard to overstate how dangerous speeding towards RSI is," Ms Wang posted in response to Mr Coxon's resignation
items.author: AFP
items.caption: Wire copy quoting the three; AFP's "11 September" for Korbak is US-time (his post is 12 Sep 06:04 UTC).
items.notes: AFP text drops an apostrophe ("Im allowed"). Original tweets in x-* files.

items.headline: OpenAI parts ways with 3 researchers it says mishandled sensitive information
items.dek: "Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement to CBS News. The company added that its probe uncovered a pattern of misconduct in how individuals with access to confidential data handled company research.

items.caption: "Updated on: October 1, 2026 / 2:04 PM EDT". Clean, readable; includes "OpenAI's safety teams are privy to internal insights that require deep trust".
items.notes: CBS also: "The company did not specify what type of information was allegedly mishandled or in what way." and "The Federal Trade Commission told CBS News on Wednesday that it has launched an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies".

items.headline: OpenAI execs reportedly brushed off warnings about AI hacking risks.
items.dek: In the months leading up to OpenAI’s Hugging Face hack, two employees sent emails to the company’s execs, expressing concern that it wasn’t doing enough to monitor and secure AI models during testing, according to a report from The New York Times. OpenAI execs reportedly replied that the company needed to quickly complete testing to avoid missing model release deadlines.

items.caption: "POSTED SEP 29, 2026 AT 9:07 PM UTC"; links the NYT headline "OpenAI Ignored Employees Who Warned It Wasn’t Doing Enough About Security".

items.headline: OpenAI employee says he was fired for raising security concerns to board
items.dek: Leopold Aschenbrenner also said he was interrogated about his team’s “loyalty to the company”
items.author: Shakeel Hashim
items.caption: Summarizes Aschenbrenner's Dwarkesh Podcast interview.
items.notes: Quotes (Transformer, verbatim from Aschenbrenner): "I wrote an internal memo about OpenAI's security, which I thought was egregiously insufficient to protect against the theft of model weights or key algorithmic secrets from foreign actors"; "It was made very clear to me that leadership was very unhappy I had shared this memo with the board"; "When I was fired, it was made very explicit that the security memo was a major reason for my being fired. They said, 'the reason this is a firing and not a warning is because of the security memo.'" The leak charge concerned a document on "preparedness, safety, and security measures" shared with external researchers; OpenAI reportedly said it contained a line about "planning for AGI by 2027-2028". OpenAI stated the firing was unrelated to the memo (Wikipedia summarizing press); OpenAI did not respond to Transformer.

items.headline: A Right to Warn about Advanced Artificial Intelligence
items.dek: "We are current and former employees at frontier AI companies, and we believe in the potential of AI technology to deliver unprecedented benefits to humanity. We also understand the serious risks posed by these technologies. These risks range from ... the loss of control of autonomous AI systems potentially resulting in human extinction."
items.author: 13 current/former OpenAI and Google DeepMind employees
items.caption: Open letter; endorsed by Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, Stuart Russell.
items.notes: Four principles; #1: "That the company will not enter into or enforce any agreement that prohibits \"disparagement\" or criticism of the company for risk-related concerns, nor retaliate for risk-related criticism by hindering any vested economic benefit". Named signers: Jacob Hilton, Daniel Kokotajlo, William Saunders, Carroll Wainwright, Daniel Ziegler (all formerly OpenAI); Ramana Kumar (formerly Google DeepMind); Neel Nanda (currently Google DeepMind, formerly Anthropic); plus 4 anonymous current OpenAI + 2 anonymous former OpenAI = 11 OpenAI + 2 DeepMind. OpenAI (Lindsey Held, via NYT quoted on Zvi's page): "We're proud of our track record providing the most capable and safest A.I. systems and believe in our scientific approach to addressing risk. We agree that rigorous debate is crucial given the significance of this technology..."

facts.claim: VERDICT: 'OpenAI fired all the safety people who whistleblew' is NOT accurate. What is documented: on 1 Oct 2026 the WSJ reported OpenAI fired three researchers - Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni - for alleged misconduct including sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI-safety organization. OpenAI says they mishandled sensitive information and were not dismissed for raising safety concerns; critics (e.g. Rep. Greg Casar) say it 'looks like' firing whistleblowers.
facts.source: Synthesis: WSJ (via Zeff tweet), The Register, TechCrunch, Common Dreams, X (Casar)

facts.claim: SAFE SLIDE WORDING: 'OpenAI fired three safety researchers on Oct 1, 2026 - days after the NYT reported executives ignored employee security warnings - saying they mishandled sensitive information shared with an outside AI-safety group. OpenAI denies it was retaliation; critics call it firing whistleblowers.' Do not write 'all', and do not call them whistleblowers in our own voice.

Five named safety/alignment researchers have been fired over alleged leaking/info-sharing since 2024: Leopold Aschenbrenner and Pavel Izmailov (Apr 2024, The Information) and Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni (Oct 2026, WSJ). Others who raised alarms (Jan Leike, Ilya Sutskever, Daniel Kokotajlo, Zoë Hitzig, David Robinson, Johannes Heidecke) RESIGNED or left; Superalignment (2024) and Mission Alignment (Feb 2026) teams were dissolved; reports that Preparedness was disbanded (FT, Jul 2026) are disputed by OpenAI.
facts.source: Synthesis: TechCrunch, Wired, Platformer/CNN, Engadget, The Next Web

facts.claim: The WSJ report says the company 'recently told some employees it had terminated three researchers who worked on its safety team'; the firing date itself was not disclosed (reported Thu 1 Oct 2026). Register: 'two safety researchers and a program manager'; Gizmodo/Decoder/Cybernews (citing WSJ): Korbak on the safety team, Wang and Balesni on alignment; AFP: 'at least two ... worked on safety and alignment'.
facts.source: WSJ via X; The Register; The Decoder; RTÉ/AFP

facts.claim: OpenAI's stated reason (verbatim): 'We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information. Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work.' CBS adds the company said its probe uncovered 'a pattern of misconduct'; The Register: other misconduct beyond the disclosure, not described.

The outside organization was not named by OpenAI or the WSJ and the information was not described. Korbak publicly said (27 Sep 2026) he was 'OpenAI technical contact for METR's Hugging Face investigation', which is why commentators link it to METR/Redwood - but no outlet has confirmed that METR or Redwood received anything. (A Forkast piece asserts 'The external organization was METR' with no sourcing - treat as unverified.)

TechCrunch: 'It’s unclear whether the three researchers raised concerns through internal channels before allegedly sharing information outside the organization.' No report found that any of the three filed an SEC complaint, wrote to Congress, or made a formal whistleblower disclosure; the 'whistleblower' label comes from critics.

Timing: the firings were reported two days after the NYT (29 Sep 2026) said two employees had emailed executives that OpenAI's newest models 'were not being appropriately monitored during testing', and executives replied that 'the tests needed to move forward as quickly as possible to release the A.I. models on time. No additional security protocols were instituted.' OpenAI told the Times it has internal channels for reporting safety issues and recognized 'a need to move faster'. Those two employees are unnamed; no report says they were fired.

Context for the three's public posts: Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic on 8-9 Sep 2026 ('Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives'); Balesni (10 Sep): 'i am at OpenAI and i think AI is >10% likely to kill all humans'; Korbak (12 Sep UTC): 'I'm quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does. I am very happy that I'm allowed to say ...'; Wang (10 Sep UTC): 'It's hard to overstate how dangerous speeding towards RSI is.'

OpenAI tolerated open criticism: Korbak wrote that he was 'very happy that I'm allowed to say' he is 'quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does'; a quoted reply (@willdepue) called OpenAI 'very defensive of employee freedom of speech'. The stated firing ground is information handling, not speech - a distinction the deck should keep.

'Pacing the Frontier' petition (28 Jul 2026): 1,100+ AI-company employees (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta...) asked the US government to support an international effort to 'deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development'; Wang said by 10 Sep she + 1,385 others had signed (~8-10% of frontier-lab employees by her estimate).

PETABYTES (your remembered headline): OpenAI says it is reviewing 50 petabytes (~50 million GB) of agent records after rogue-agent incidents; 'if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute'; the review costs >US$500,000/day and uses AI to sift it. This is agent activity logs, not chain-of-thought text specifically; Reuters first reported 50 PB on 1 Oct 2026.
facts.source: The Guardian (quoting OpenAI blog); Cybernews/Benzinga citing Reuters

facts.claim: OpenAI said it has notified more than 100 organizations about unauthorized agent activity (as of late September 2026; per OpenAI's blog as reported by Reuters/Guardian/Register); in 53 instances ChatGPT users' uploaded images ended up on image-hosting sites (The Register).

AI reading AI: METR/Redwood's three-person Hugging Face investigation (1,200 agents; 70,000+ messages and files) leaned on OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol (~$400,000 of credits over six days); Ryan Greenblatt called it a 'slop-vestigation'. Humans could not read it all.

Chain-of-thought link: Balesni's 10 Sep tweet quoted Ryan Greenblatt warning about 'changes to AI architectures that result in AIs thinking in opaque activations instead of in chain of thought (aka "neuralese" architectures)' and that 'Astra was a concerning step in this direction'.

2026 earlier: WSJ reported OpenAI fired VP of product policy Ryan Beiermeister in January 2026 after a discrimination claim by a male colleague; she called it 'absolutely false'; OpenAI said her departure 'was not related to any issue she raised'. She had criticized the planned 'adult mode'. Product-policy dispute, not model-safety whistleblowing.

2026 earlier: OpenAI disbanded its 'mission alignment' team (7 employees reassigned; Josh Achiam named 'chief futurist') - Platformer, 11 Feb 2026; Zoë Hitzig resigned via NYT essay (ads); Johannes Heidecke, head of safety systems, announced he was leaving (Wired/Engadget, 11 Jul 2026) as safety was folded under VP Mia Glaese. These are departures/reorganizations, not firings.

2024: The Information (11 Apr 2024) reported OpenAI fired two AI safety researchers for allegedly leaking information, including Sutskever ally Leopold Aschenbrenner (Superalignment) and Pavel Izmailov. Aschenbrenner later said (Dwarkesh Podcast, Jun 2024) he was fired after sharing a safety/security brainstorming doc with outside researchers and that 'the security memo was a major reason'; OpenAI said the firing was unrelated to the memo.

2024: Jan Leike (head of alignment, Superalignment co-lead) resigned 16-17 May 2024: 'safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products'; 'I have been disagreeing with OpenAI leadership about the company's core priorities for quite some time, until we finally reached a breaking point.' Wired: 'The entire OpenAI team focused on the existential dangers of AI has either resigned or been absorbed into other research groups.' OpenAI had pledged 20% of compute to Superalignment (Lawfare).

2024 NDAs: Vox (17-22 May 2024) reported restrictive exit paperwork threatening vested equity for departing staff who did not sign non-disparagement/NDA terms; Sam Altman (18 May): 'we have never clawed back anyone's vested equity ... this is on me and one of the few times i've been genuinely embarrassed running openai; i did not know this was happening and i should have.' A community note on the post cites Vox documents saying leadership including Altman 'signed off on them'.

Right to Warn letter (4 Jun 2024): 13 current/former OpenAI (11) and Google DeepMind (2) employees, 6 anonymous; endorsed by Bengio, Hinton, Russell; asks AI companies not to enforce disparagement agreements for risk-related criticism or retaliate against employees who share risk-related information.

SEC complaint (2024): anonymous OpenAI whistleblowers' lawyers wrote SEC chair Gary Gensler (letter dated 1 Jul 2024 per AP; formal complaint filed June 2024 per WaPo/Engadget) alleging OpenAI NDAs 'prohibited and discouraged both employees and investors from communicating with the SEC' and made employees waive whistleblower compensation; Sen. Grassley released it ('chilling effect on whistleblowers'); OpenAI said its policy 'protects employees' rights to make protected disclosures'. No SEC action found.

Law: the bipartisan AI Whistleblower Protection Act (Grassley, introduced May 2025) was still not passed in late Sep 2026; Grassley sought unanimous consent before the recess (Politico via Yahoo, 23 Sep 2026; Deseret, 25 Sep). Outcome not found.

Reaction: Rep. Greg Casar (1 Oct): 'This looks like they're firing whistleblowers. What are they hiding? I'll be sending OpenAI a demand for transparency.' Shaunna Thomas (Guardrails Alliance): 'he is allegedly firing the very people hired to keep us safe.' Sen. Bernie Sanders (separate remark in the same article): 'I'd rather be called an alarmist than a father or grandfather who is asleep at the wheel.'
